slides.title: From shell to kernel
slides.main: We go top down: programs, calls, kernel, hardware. We start with files.

captions: On top the shell and programs: what you work with every day
Below them, system calls: the only door into the kernel
The kernel manages processes, memory, files and network
And under the kernel, the hardware we covered in the architecture book

slides.title: One tree
slides.main: All files grow from one root; a path reads from root to leaf.

captions: One root: no drive letters, everything grows from the slash
Settings, homes, data, programs: ordinary directories on disk
proc, sys and dev are not disk: they let you talk to the kernel
A path reads from root to leaf; each slash is a step deeper

frames.text: blue: windows into the kernel, not disk but system state

slides.title: Everything is a file
slides.main: Open, read, write, close: the same for a file, a terminal and a socket.

captions: The first letter in "ls -l" tells you what it is: file or directory
A link is also a file, with a path stored inside
Block and character devices, sockets, pipes: all in the tree
The same calls apply to any of them

frames.text: a link is a file with a path inside
devices, sockets and pipes are files too

slides.title: Inode and name
slides.sub: A file is an inode; the name lives in the directory
slides.main: Metadata and block pointers live in the inode, the name in the directory.

captions: A directory is a file with a table of "name and inode number"
An inode stores owner, permissions, size, times
And pointers to data blocks; the name is not in the inode
Renaming edits a directory row and leaves the data alone

slides.title: Hard and symbolic links
slides.sub: Two ways to have several paths
slides.main: Hard: another name for an inode; symbolic: a file with a path inside.

captions: Usually an inode has one name and the link count is one
A hard link is a second name for the same inode; the count goes to two
A symbolic link is a separate file holding a path to a name
Count zero: data freed, and the symbolic link dangles

slides.title: Open file
slides.sub: A descriptor keeps the inode alive
slides.main: While a file is open, deleting its name does not free the space.

captions: open returns a descriptor: a number in the process table
rm removes the name, but the inode lives while the file is open
The disk isn't freed, although the file is "gone" from the directory
close frees the inode and blocks: the space is back

slides.title: Mounting
slides.sub: Disks become branches of the tree
slides.main: mount attaches a file system to a directory; the kernel picks the longest mount point.

captions: The home directory is empty for now, and the second disk has its own files
mount attaches the disk to a directory, and its tree becomes a branch of the main one
Walking a path, you cross the boundary without noticing
The kernel keeps a table of mount points and takes the longest match

slides.title: Journal and copy-on-write
slides.main: ext4 and XFS keep a journal; Btrfs writes a new copy and switches a pointer.

captions: ext4 and XFS first write the intent to the journal
After commit the change is applied in place, and a crash is cured by replay
Btrfs writes a new version of the block into free space
One pointer move and the new version is live; the old one serves as a snapshot

frames.text: 1. write to the journal what we plan to do
2. after commit apply it; after a crash replay

slides.title: Blocks and inodes
slides.sub: Space runs out in two ways
slides.main: Check both space and inodes: df -h and df -i.

captions: A file takes a whole number of blocks, usually four kilobytes
A tiny file still eats a block: this is tail waste
Inodes are issued in advance, and small files can exhaust them
So check both space and inodes: df -h and df -i

frames.text: the disk is split into blocks; a file takes a whole number of them
a one-byte file takes a whole block
millions of small files: inodes ran out before space
"No space left" error, though gigabytes are free

slides.title: How the kernel finds a file
slides.main: The VFS walks the path, caches entries and hands back a descriptor.

captions: The path is split into components, and the kernel walks them one by one
Each needs a directory entry: first in the cache, on a miss from disk
The last entry points to the file's inode
The kernel creates an open file and gives the process its number
